[Monte Carlo integration](monte-carlo-integration.qmd#from-a-weighted-sum-to-a-draw-average)
gave us a simple recipe: draw from the posterior and average. But that recipe
assumed the operation we do not yet know how to perform. If we could already
generate independent draws from an arbitrary posterior, most of the remaining
computational problem would be solved.

Suppose instead that we can draw from an easier distribution. We will call
this distribution the **proposal distribution** and denote its density by
$q$. The proposal might visit some parameter values more often than the
posterior would and other values less often. **Importance sampling** corrects
that mismatch by attaching a weight to every proposal draw.

The basic idea is easiest to see with two regions. Suppose the proposal sends
half of its draws to region $A$, while the posterior assigns only one quarter
of its probability there. Draws in $A$ occur twice as often as they should, so
each receives a relative weight of $(1/4)/(1/2)=1/2$. Suppose the proposal
sends the other half to region $B$, while the posterior assigns three quarters
of its probability there. Draws in $B$ occur too rarely, so each receives a
relative weight of $(3/4)/(1/2)=3/2$. Weighting corrects the frequencies
created by the proposal.

We will now derive the same correction for a continuous parameter. We require
the proposal pairs $(\mu^{(1)},\lambda^{(1)}),\ldots,
(\mu^{(S)},\lambda^{(S)})$ to be independent draws from $q$, where
$\lambda=\log\sigma$. We also require $q(\mu,\lambda)>0$ everywhere that the posterior contribution we
want to average is nonzero. After deriving those requirements, we will inspect
what happens when the weights become concentrated on a few draws.

## Reweighting a proposal

For target density $f$, proposal density $q$, and function $g$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_f[g(\mu,\lambda)]
&=
\int\!\!\int g(\mu,\lambda)
\frac{f(\mu,\lambda)}{q(\mu,\lambda)}q(\mu,\lambda)
\,\mathrm d\lambda\,\mathrm d\mu\\
&=
\mathbb{E}_q[g(\mu,\lambda)w(\mu,\lambda)],
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $w(\mu,\lambda)=f(\mu,\lambda)/q(\mu,\lambda)$ is the
[**importance weight**](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/inverse-problems-and-data-assimilation/monte-carlo-sampling-and-importance-sampling/AEE4AC4E63548DC6A732013B571841D8). The first
equality multiplies the integrand by
$q(\mu,\lambda)/q(\mu,\lambda)$. It requires
$q(\mu,\lambda)>0$ wherever
$g(\mu,\lambda)f(\mu,\lambda)$ contributes to the target integral.
This is the support condition: a proposal cannot reweight draws from a region
it never visits.

If the target is known only as
$\widetilde f(\mu,\lambda)=Zf(\mu,\lambda)$, normalized weights

$$
\widetilde w^{(s)}
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)})/
q(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)})}
{\sum_{r=1}^S\widetilde f(\mu^{(r)},\lambda^{(r)})/
q(\mu^{(r)},\lambda^{(r)})}
$$

remove the shared unknown constant. The self-normalized estimator is

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\sum_{s=1}^S\widetilde w^{(s)}g(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)}).
$$

It is generally biased at finite $S$, but consistent under the required support and integrability conditions.

The first line of the derivation is worth reading from right to left. The
factor $q(\mu,\lambda)\,\mathrm d\lambda\,\mathrm d\mu$ tells us how proposal draws are distributed.
The ratio $f(\mu,\lambda)/q(\mu,\lambda)$ removes the proposal's relative frequency and
replaces it with the target's relative frequency. We have changed the
distribution used for averaging without changing the integral itself.

The ordinary estimator
$S^{-1}\sum_s g(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)})
f(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)})/q(\mu^{(s)},\lambda^{(s)})$ is unbiased when the
**normalized** target density $f$ is available and the expectation exists.
Self-normalization replaces the unavailable target normalizer by the random
sum of raw weights. That ratio creates finite-sample bias, though it converges
to the correct expectation under the stated conditions.

## Assessing importance weights

The code reconstructs the same posterior grid used on the preceding page. It
then draws 30,000 values from a bivariate $t_5$ proposal centered at the grid
mean with scale $1.5\widehat\Sigma$. These settings are chosen to cover this
posterior; they make no claim about a distribution of linguistic observations.

How do we choose this proposal? The grid gives us a center and a covariance
matrix that describe the posterior's main location, scale, and orientation.
Multiplying the covariance by $1.5$ spreads proposal draws farther around that
region. Using five degrees of freedom gives the proposal heavier tails than a
normal distribution, so it reaches distant values more often. These settings
serve the approximation. The Provo observations do not determine them. A
deliberately narrow normal proposal would have full support but would still
produce a few very large weights and a poor finite approximation.

```{r}
#| label: provo-importance-sampling
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
nu <- 4
prior_scale <- 2 * sd(y)

log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
  maximum <- max(x)
  maximum + log(sum(exp(x - maximum)))
}
log_posterior_pair <- function(parameter_pair) {
  mu <- parameter_pair[1]; sigma <- exp(parameter_pair[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) + parameter_pair[2]
}
mode_fit <- optim(c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
                  function(parameter_pair) -log_posterior_pair(parameter_pair),
                  method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
                  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L))
local_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(mode_fit$hessian)))
grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(mode_fit$par[1] - 7 * local_sd[1],
           mode_fit$par[1] + 7 * local_sd[1], length.out = 321L),
  log_sigma = seq(mode_fit$par[2] - 7 * local_sd[2],
                  mode_fit$par[2] + 7 * local_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
)
grid$log_kernel <- apply(grid, 1, log_posterior_pair)
grid$weight <- exp(grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(grid$log_kernel))
grid_mean <- colSums(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")] * grid$weight)
centered <- sweep(as.matrix(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")]),
                  2, grid_mean, "-")
grid_covariance <- crossprod(centered * sqrt(grid$weight))

rmvt <- function(n, location, scale, df) {
  dimension <- length(location)
  normal <- matrix(rnorm(n * dimension), nrow = n)
  standard <- sqrt(rchisq(n, df = df) / df)
  sweep(normal %*% chol(scale), 1, standard, "/") +
    matrix(location, nrow = n, ncol = dimension, byrow = TRUE)
}
dmvt_log <- function(x, location, scale, df) {
  dimension <- length(location)
  centered <- sweep(x, 2, location, "-")
  inverse <- solve(scale)
  quadratic <- rowSums((centered %*% inverse) * centered)
  log_determinant <- determinant(scale, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus[1]
  lgamma((df + dimension) / 2) - lgamma(df / 2) -
    .5 * (dimension * log(df * pi) + log_determinant) -
    .5 * (df + dimension) * log1p(quadratic / df)
}

set.seed(2026101803)
S <- 30000L
proposal_df <- 5
proposal_scale <- 1.5 * grid_covariance
proposal_pairs <- rmvt(S, grid_mean, proposal_scale, proposal_df)
log_weight <- apply(proposal_pairs, 1, log_posterior_pair) -
  dmvt_log(proposal_pairs, grid_mean, proposal_scale, proposal_df)
weight <- exp(log_weight - log_sum_exp(log_weight))

importance_ess <- 1 / sum(weight^2)
summary <- data.frame(
  mean_mu = sum(weight * proposal_pairs[, 1]),
  probability_mu_positive = sum(weight * (proposal_pairs[, 1] > 0)),
  mean_exp_mu = sum(weight * exp(proposal_pairs[, 1])),
  raw_weight_ess = importance_ess,
  largest_weight = max(weight),
  top_100_weight_share = sum(sort(weight, decreasing = TRUE)[1:100])
)
stopifnot(length(y) == 55L, abs(sum(weight) - 1) < 1e-12)
summary
```

The raw-weight effective sample size,

$$
\operatorname{ESS}_w
=
\frac{1}{\sum_{s=1}^S(\widetilde w^{(s)})^2},
$$

is `r format(round(importance_ess), big.mark = ",")` from 30,000 proposal draws. It equals the raw draw count when the normalized weights are equal and approaches one when one draw dominates. The later [effective-sample-size page](effective-sample-size.qmd#from-autocorrelation-to-ess) develops a different ESS for dependent Markov-chain averages; neither quantity is the number of Provo passages.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-importance-weights
#| fig-cap: "Proposal draws for the passage-level Student-t model. The accent marks the one percent with the largest normalized weights."
proposal_draws <- data.frame(
  mu = proposal_pairs[, 1], sigma = exp(proposal_pairs[, 2]), weight = weight
)
weight_cutoff <- quantile(weight, .99)

proposal_opacity <- .16
weighted_opacity <- .65
ggplot(proposal_draws, aes(mu, sigma)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey70", alpha = proposal_opacity, size = .55) +
  geom_point(data = subset(proposal_draws, weight >= weight_cutoff),
             color = "#8B1A1A", alpha = weighted_opacity, size = .8) +
  labs(x = "Passage-level contrast (mu)",
       y = "Passage contrast scale (sigma)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The proposal must cover every target region of positive probability. Shared support is not sufficient for efficiency: if $q$ places little mass in an important target region, a few weights dominate. The largest weight and the mass in the largest 100 weights diagnose that realized concentration but cannot prove that an unseen tail was covered.

The proposal distribution is a computational device. Before weighting, its
draw frequencies describe the proposal we chose. After weighting, those
frequencies approximate the passage-level Student-t posterior. The proposal
therefore carries no additional prior or empirical claim about passage
contrasts.

## Recap and forward link

1. Importance sampling rewrites a target expectation as a proposal expectation through a density ratio.
2. The proposal must cover every target region relevant to the integrand.
3. Self-normalization removes an unknown target constant at the cost of finite-sample bias.
4. Weight concentration, not the raw proposal count, determines practical efficiency.

The [Markov-chain page](markov-chains.qmd#transition-and-stationary-distributions) next replaces independent proposal draws with a dependent transition sequence.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does self-normalization remove the target normalizer?
2. What fails when $q(\mu,\lambda)=0$ in a target region?
3. Why can full support still yield poor efficiency?
4. What does $\operatorname{ESS}_w$ count in this calculation?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Every raw weight contains the same unknown multiplicative target constant, which cancels when weights are divided by their sum. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The weight ratio is undefined there, and proposal draws can never represent that positive-probability part of the target. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A proposal may have full support but place very little mass in an important target region, causing a few extreme weights to dominate. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. $\operatorname{ESS}_w$ is the number of equally weighted proposal draws with roughly comparable weight information; it is not a passage count or a Markov-chain ESS. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
